Soldiers of an army patrol from the Lince company; officers convicted in 2016 by Peru's National Criminal Court
Villagers, including women, older people and children; the count is 62 in the Truth and Reconciliation Commission report and 69 in other sources

Ayacucho, the heartland of the Shining Path insurgency

content.p: On 14 August 1985, soldiers from two army patrols rounded up the people of Accomarca, a small farming village in the high Andes of Ayacucho department in south-central Peru. They locked the villagers into two houses, fired into them, threw grenades and set the buildings alight. Many of the dead were women, older people and children. The village was one of the places where the army's counterinsurgency against the Shining Path guerrillas turned on civilians who had no link to the rebels, according to the country's Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

The number killed has never been settled. The commission counted 62 victims. A list of 69 names published in the press at the time, which later reports repeated, gave 69. The Center for Justice and Accountability, which worked on the case in the United States, also gave 69. Because the bodies were burned, the exact figure was hard to confirm, and a 2016 report from the Instituto Humanitas Unisinos gives the official count as 61.

Peru's internal conflict ran from 1980 to 2000. The Shining Path, a Maoist group, fought the state from its strongholds in the Ayacucho highlands, and the army and police answered with operations that often fell on the rural population. The commission described how the group sought to replace local authorities with its own "popular committees", and said that authorities in Accomarca who refused to give up their posts were killed in 1982.

The army unit involved was the Lince company, based in Huamanga. Its operation in August 1985 was called Plan Operativo Huancayoc, which the commission said was planned by the military organisation of the Security Sub-Zone No. 5 and carried out with little regard for the lives of innocent civilians. The commission concluded that the killings were carried out with disregard for the lives of innocent civilians, and that the villagers had no link to the guerrillas. Al Jazeera reported that, despite finding no evidence against the villagers, a unit led by Second Lieutenant Telmo Hurtado carried out the killings.

According to IPS, the plan's goal was to eliminate Shining Path rebels supposedly hiding in the area, and Major José Daniel Williams Zapata, who commanded the Lince company, took part in designing it.

Accounts of the morning of 14 August come mainly from soldiers who later testified and from relatives who survived. A former soldier, José Contreras, told the court that the patrol forced the villagers into one small house after questioning them. In his account, Lieutenant Hurtado fired on the people inside, threw a grenade, and then ordered the house burned. When an 80-year-old villager, Juliana Baldeón, appeared, the lieutenant ordered her shot, and she was killed on the third shot, according to the same testimony reported by IPS.

A second former soldier, Francisco Marcañaupa, said the villagers were gathered and that he saw Hurtado open fire before a grenade was thrown in. Marcañaupa told the court that Hurtado had described Accomarca as a "red zone" dominated by the Shining Path, and that the patrol had to attack those people. Contreras also told the court that interrogation was part of the method: the aim, he said, was to make villagers confess to supporting the guerrillas or to name others. Five women were stripped, put in water and questioned, he testified.

Survivors who were children at the time described the same sequence. Two girls, about 12 and 13 years old by the Center for Justice and Accountability's account, hid and watched soldiers corral the villagers into two buildings, fire into them and throw grenades. Their mothers and siblings were among the dead, according to that organisation. A man who was 14 at the time, now the leader of a group representing the families, was in the fields with his father that morning. They came back to a silent village that smelled of burned flesh. His mother, an 8-year-old brother and a 6-year-old sister were among those killed, Al Jazeera reported.

The killings did not end the pressure on people who had seen them. The commission said the military killed seven witnesses in the days that followed. Among the dead on 8 September 1985, according to a digitized report on the case, were Brígida Pérez Chávez and her son Alejandro Baldeón. The next day soldiers from the Vilcashuamán garrison detained Martín Baldeón Ayala, then 66, and took him to the base.

Congress responded slowly. On 11 September 1985 the upper chamber of Congress appointed an investigating commission under Javier Valle Riestra, with a mandate to look into the Pucayacu and Accomarca massacres. Two days later, the deputy Fernando Olivera visited Accomarca and found the bodies of five people hidden in niches in the village cemetery. The digitized report describes them as shot, with no rigor mortis.

The case first went to military justice. In March 1986 the Supreme Court sent it there. The military court acquitted Hurtado of homicide and negligence but sentenced him to six years for abuse of authority, with 500 soles in civil damages to the victims' families, and the other soldiers were acquitted. A higher military body confirmed that ruling seven years later, according to the APRODEH account of the case.

By 2008, according to the families' lawyer, Karim Ninaquispe, the crime had gone unpunished for nearly a quarter of a century. Testimony from former soldiers pointed further up the chain. Ninaquispe told IPS that one soldier's account showed that Williams Zapata knew of the clean-up the day after the killings, and that General Wilfredo Mori, who commanded the military political front, had authorised the patrols. Those were the lawyer's conclusions from the testimony, not findings of a court.
content.h2: Exile, arrest and the American lawsuits
content.p: For many years justice was out of reach for the officers. A 1995 amnesty law, passed under President Alberto Fujimori, shielded security forces from prosecution. Al Jazeera reported that the law was repealed in 2001, and only then could effective judicial investigations begin.

In the meantime, Telmo Hurtado and Juan Rivera Rondón had moved to the United States. Hurtado was arrested there in March 2007 by immigration agents. In 2007 the Center for Justice and Accountability filed two civil suits in federal court, one against Rivera Rondón in Maryland and one against Hurtado in Florida. A federal judge entered a default judgment against Hurtado, ordering him to pay 37 million dollars to two survivors, who had been 12 and 13 at the time. IPS, writing in August 2008, dated the order to 4 March; the Center's own statement on the 2016 verdict gives the year as 2007. The Center said it was the first time anyone had been held accountable for the Accomarca killings.

The two men then faced the immigration process. The Center for Justice and Accountability says the United States deported Rivera Rondón to Peru in 2008; IPS, writing in August 2008, described him as extradited from Maryland. Hurtado was extradited to Peru in 2011. The Center described that extradition as the first time US authorities had honored an extradition request for torture and genocide. Williams Zapata, who was then in Washington, had to fly to Lima every two months to sign in at court, IPS reported in 2008.

The trial ran before the National Criminal Court in Lima. The verdict came on 1 September 2016, after a trial that the PeruReports described as lasting about six years. The court found the defendants guilty of grave human rights violations. The Center for Justice and Accountability says the court found its clients and seven others guilty; PeruReports reported 16 former soldiers sentenced, and the Instituto Humanitas Unisinos report said ten military men were convicted. The sources differ on the number, and the figure given here follows each report.

The sentences also differ. PeruReports gave Hurtado 23 years and General Wilfredo Mori 25 years. Three lieutenants received 24 to 25 years, and eleven soldiers 10 years, according to the same report. Six men were acquitted for lack of evidence, including General José Williams. The Center for Justice and Accountability gives 24 years for Hurtado and 23 for Rivera Rondón. PeruReports also reported punitive damages of 44,000 dollars for each of the victims' families.

The prosecutor, Luis Landa, told El Comercio after a 15-hour deliberation that the killings were not "an isolated incident from Telmo Hurtado" but "the result of a systematic pattern." He said there had been a plan designed by the security forces in the area and carried out by the patrols, and that it amounted to a crime against humanity, PeruReports quoted him as saying. The judgment, as quoted by the Instituto Humanitas Unisinos report, described the crimes as part of an illegal anti-terrorism policy.

Hurtado had admitted his part in the massacre in 2012, PeruReports reported. He was the only convicted soldier in custody when the verdict came; the others were fugitives with arrest warrants, according to the same report.

The convictions were challenged. In September 2018, the Center for Justice and Accountability reported, Peru's Supreme Court refused to void the convictions of Hurtado and Rivera Rondón, along with those of Mori Orso and Gonzales Feria.

Exhuming the dead took decades. The victims were buried together in a single grave close to the house where they died. On 20 April 2022, the Center reported, 37 identified bodies were returned to families for a dignified burial. Al Jazeera described a formal burial that year with a white coffin for each of the dead. Some coffins held only bone fragments, and others held clothes. Where nothing could be recovered, an empty coffin was buried instead. The families' leader told Al Jazeera that the remains of 18 victims had not been found and that there were not enough resources to continue the DNA analysis.

On 8 July 2025 the Criminal Court, according to the Center for Justice and Accountability, suspended the prison sentence of Mori Orzo because he was over 80. Families were still demanding reparations and the search for the missing, the Center said.

In July 2025 Peru's Congress approved a bill granting amnesty to members of the armed forces and the police accused of crimes during the conflict. Human rights organisations told Al Jazeera that it could erase about 156 convictions and more than 600 ongoing investigations. It would also give "humanitarian" amnesty to officials convicted of such crimes who were over 70. At the time of that report the bill awaited the decision of President Dina Boluarte, who could sign it into law or send it back to Congress.

The families' group, Al Jazeera reported, says its members feel "outraged and betrayed" by Congress. Jo-Marie Burt, a George Mason University professor who has studied the violence, called the bill "a dramatic setback". She said Peru is among a handful of Latin American countries that has brought some of the most emblematic cases from its armed conflict to trial.

For the families in Accomarca, the case has been a matter of decades. The killings took place in one day, but the search for who gave the orders, the convictions and the fight to keep them standing have run for more than forty years.
